content: The project control process 16 ❑ Setting a baseline plan ❑ Measuring progress and performance ❑ Comparing plan against actual ❑ Taking actions ➢ Time and budgets are quantitative measures of performance. ➢ Measurement of time performance is relatively easy and obvious. That is, is the critical path early, on schedule or late; is the slack of near-critical paths decreasing to cause new critical activities? ➢ Measuring performance against budget (e.g. money, units in place, labour hours) is more difficult and is not simply a case of comparing actual versus budget.

title: ENGG4800_Lecture_8_Week_8_S1_2026 - page 25
content: Earned value cost/schedule system 25 Development of an earned value (EV) cost/schedule system ❑The EV system starts with the time-phased costs that provide the project budget baseline - the planned budgeted value of the work scheduled (PV). ❑Given this time-phased baseline, comparisons are made with actual and planned schedules and costs using EV. ❑The EV approach provides the missing links not found in conventional cost-budget systems. ❑At any point in time, a status report can be developed for the project.

title: ENGG4800_Lecture_8_Week_8_S1_2026 - page 26
content: Earned value cost/schedule system 26 Steps of integrating cost/schedule system Step 1 - Define the work using a WBS. This step involves developing documents that include the following information: ➢ scope ➢ work packages ➢ deliverables ➢ organisation units ➢ resources ➢ budgets for each work package Step 2 - Develop work and resource schedule. ➢ Schedule resources to activities ➢ Time-phase work packages into a network Step 3 - Develop a time-phase budget using work packages included in an activity. ➢ The cumulative values of these budgets will become the baseline and will be called the planned budgeted cost of the work scheduled (PV). ➢ The sum should equal the budgeted amounts for all the work packages in the cost accounts.

title: ENGG4800_Lecture_8_Week_8_S1_2026 - page 27
content: Earned value cost/schedule system 27 Steps of integrating cost/schedule system Step 4 - At the work package level, collect the actual costs for the work performed. These costs will be called the actual cost of the work completed (AC). Collect per cent complete and multiply this times the original budget amount for the value of the work completed. These values will be called earned values (EV). ➢ EV is the per cent of the original budget that has been earned by actual work completed. Step 5 - Compute ➢ Schedule variance (SV = EV – PV) and ➢ Cost variance (CV = EV – AC). Prepare hierarchical status reports for each level of management—from work package manager to customer or project manager.

title: ENGG4800_Lecture_8_Week_8_S1_2026 - page 28
content: Earned value cost/schedule system 28 Steps of integrating cost/schedule system ❑ Schedule variance (SV = EV – PV) ❑ Cost variance (CV = EV – AC) Cost variance tells us if the work accomplished costs more or less than was planned at any point over the life of the project. If labour and materials have not been separated, cost variance should be reviewed carefully to isolate the cause to either labour or materials—or to both. Schedule variance presents an overall assessment of all work packages in the project scheduled to date. It is important to note schedule variance contains no critical path information. Schedule variance measures progress in dollars rather than time units. The only accurate method for determining the true time progress of the project is to compare the project network schedule against the actual network schedule to measure if the project is on time

title: ENGG4800_Lecture_8_Week_8_S1_2026 - page 29
content: Earned value cost/schedule system 29 Methods of variation analysis ❑ Schedule variance (SV = EV – PV) ❑ Cost variance (CV = EV – AC) The method for measuring accomplishments centres on two key computations: ❑ Comparing EV with the expected schedule value (Schedule variance) ❑ Comparing EV with the actual costs (Cost variance) ➢ Planned cost of the work scheduled (PV) ➢ Budgeted cost of the work completed (EV) ➢ Actual cost of the work completed (AC)

title: ENGG4800_Lecture_8_Week_8_S1_2026 - page 30

The graph also focuses on • EV (Earned value) • PV (Planned budgeted value) • AC (Actual cost) • what remains to be accomplished • Any favourable or unfavourable trends. Report date

title: ENGG4800_Lecture_8_Week_8_S1_2026 - page 31
content: Earned value cost/schedule system 31 Methods of variation analysis • At the end of period 25, 75 per cent of the work was scheduled to be accomplished. At the end of period 25, the value of the work accomplished is 50 per cent. • The actual cost of the work completed to date is $340, or 85 per cent of the total project budget. The graph suggests the project will have about an 18 per cent cost overrun and be five times units late. • The current status of the project shows the cost variance (CV) to be over budget by $140 (EV – AC = 200 – 340 = –140). • The schedule variance (SV) is negative $100 (EV – PV = 200 – 300 = –100), which suggests the project is behind schedule. ~18% over run

title: ENGG4800_Lecture_8_Week_8_S1_2026 - page 33
content: Indexes to monitor progress 33 Performance Index Cost performance index (CPI) = EV AC Schedule performance index (SPI) = EV PV If CPI is 0.7 $0.70 worth of work planned to date has been completed for each $1.00 actually spent—an unfavourable situation indeed. The CPI is the most accepted and used index. It has been tested over time and found to be the most accurate, reliable and stable. If SPI is 0.8 The schedule index indicates $0.80 worth of work has been accomplished for each $1.00 worth of scheduled work to date. Project Per cent Complete Index

title: ENGG4800_Lecture_8_Week_8_S1_2026 - page 34
content: Indexes to monitor progress 34 Performance Index Per cent complete index (PCIB) = EV BAC = 160 320 = 0.5 (50%) Project Per cent Complete Index PCIB is 0.50 (50%) PCIB indicates the work accomplished represents 50 per cent of the total budgeted (BAC) dollars to date. PCIC is 0.4 (40%) PCIC views per cent complete in terms of actual dollars spent to accomplish the work to date and the actual expected dollars for the completed project (EAC). For example, at the end of period 7 the staff re-estimates that the EAC will be 575 instead of 320. BAC = $320 Per cent complete index (PCIC) = AC EAC = 230 575 = 0.4 (40%)

title: ENGG4800_Practical 4 (updated) - page 1
content: ENGG 4800 1 ENGG4800 ENGG4800 - Practical Four Task Information Robin Lane and top management have approved the schedule generated at the end of Part 3. As the project schedule is now approved , it can be set as a baseline – from which point the schedule can be progressed through and deviated from. Useful Terms Here is a reminder of useful terminology. Term About PV / BCWS Planned Value, also known as Budgeted Cost of Work Scheduled (BCWS) EV / BCWP Earned Value, also known as the Budgeted Cost of Work Performed (BCWP) AC / ACWP Actual Cost, also known as Actual Cost of Work Performed (ACWP) SV Schedule Variance in Cost Terms (BCWP – BCWS) it is the difference in cost between the current progress and the baseline activity. CV Cost Variance is the difference between how much the activity should have cost and how much it actually cost (BCWP - ACWP). EAC Estimate at Completion, expected total cost of activity. BAC Baseline Cost, the total planned cost for an activity. CPI Cost performance index. Typically, BCWP ÷ ACWP. PCI Percent Complete Indices

content: What is Vector DB? 4/6/2026 7 • Traditional DB: discrete, scalar data types (numbers and strings) in rows/ columns. • Vector DB: high-dim vector data (embeddings) for similarity search

title: INFS7205_Lecture6_High Dimensional Indexing-v1 - page 8
content: Why Similarity Search? 4/6/2026 8 • If we stick to exact kNN search… (recall in Lec1, as dimension goes up, volume grows exponentially, traditional indexing (e.g., KD-trees collapses into O(N) linear scans)

title: INFS7205_Lecture6_High Dimensional Indexing-v1 - page 9
content: Why Similarity Search? 4/6/2026 9 Flat Index (Brute Force) • Flat indices are a direct representation of the vector embedding • Deliver the best accuracy of all indexing methods, but notoriously slow • Search is exhaustive: it’s performed from the query vector acrossevery single vector embedding and distances are calculated for each pair. • If we stick to exact kNN search… Query Vector Query Vector（k=3)

title: INFS7205_Lecture6_High Dimensional Indexing-v1 - page 10
content: Approximate Nearest Neighbour Search (ANN) 4/6/2026 10 • Allowed to return points, whose distance from the query is at most 𝑐times the distance from the query to its nearest points • Faster Search: billion-scale data on memory • Trade-offs: runtime, accuracy, memory-consumption

title: INFS7205_Lecture6_High Dimensional Indexing-v1 - page 11

Break down the knowledge base (the "corpus" of documents) into smaller chunks of text, usually no more than a few hundred tokens; 2. Create TF-IDF encodings and semantic embeddings for these chunks; 3. Use BM25 to find top chunks based on exact matches; 4. Use embeddings to find top chunks based on semantic similarity; 5. content: Take-home Message • Naïve RAG is brittle: chunking, retrieval, and ranking all matter . • Better RAG is a pipeline design problem: hybrid search, reranking, and query planning improve evidence quality. • Multimodal RAG is not text RAG with images attached: preserving original visual evidence matters. • Not all knowledge should be retrieved online: some can be compiled into LLM Wiki / graph memory. • Future systems will be hybrid: retrieve fresh/raw evidence, compile stable/reusable knowledge.
